summary:
Bayburt is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework, in which hostility toward LGBT people has been converted from residual prejudice into explicit state policy. The draft legislative package reported in October 2025 contained no provisions specific to any province, and no Bayburt-specific ordinance, court decision or enforcement practice is sourced for this entry. The national picture therefore applies in Bayburt unchanged.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus justice package, described as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend Turkey's penal and civil codes so as to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. Participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would be a criminal offence carrying penalties of up to four years in prison. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require proof of permanent infertility, and would punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. As of the reporting date the measure had not been passed, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has been institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner created a climate encouraging human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Street-level enforcement illustrates how the pending law is already applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. The Kaos GL findings on the 'Year of the Family' banner and senior officials' hate speech sit within that same framing.

Compared with jurisdictions where document checks are routine but do not compare presentation against markers, Turkey's combination of mandatory original-ID carriage for foreigners, GBT stops, and a pending criminalisation package makes checkpoint encounters a qualitatively higher outing risk than the regional norm.
